modules.title: Pitch, Notation, and the Staff
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Moment: The First Note That Won’t Stay in Your Head  

You’re sitting at a piano‑bench, a piece of sheet music spread before you. The first measure shows a single, black‑filled note perched on the second line of the treble staff, a **quarter‑note** with a **sharp** sign attached. Your fingers hover, but you’re not sure whether that line represents G, A, or B, nor whether the sharp raises the pitch by a half step or cancels a previous flat.  

That split‑second hesitation is the exact point where **pitch, notation, and the staff** intersect. Mastering the visual language of the staff eliminates the guesswork, letting you translate symbols into sound instantly. The following sections break down every element you need to read and write simple melodies fluently—lines, spaces, clefs, note values, rests, accidentals, and ledger lines.

---

## The Five‑Line Staff and Its Clefs  

### The Five‑Line Staff  

The **staff** (or stave) is the foundational grid on which music is written. It consists of **five parallel horizontal lines**, each separated by a **space**. Together, the lines and spaces form a series of pitch positions that repeat every octave.  

- **Lines** are counted from bottom to top: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5.  
- **Spaces** are likewise counted: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 (the space between lines 1‑2 is space 1, etc.).  

The staff alone tells you *where* a note sits, but not *what* pitch it represents—this is where clefs come in.

### The Treble Clef (G Clef)  

The **treble clef** curls around the second line from the bottom. Its stylized “G” indicates that this line is **G₄** (the G above middle C). From that anchor point, every other line and space is a fixed interval away:

| Position | Pitch (Scientific Pitch Notation) |
|----------|-----------------------------------|
| Line 1   | E₄                               |
| Space 1  | F₄                               |
| Line 2   | **G₄** (anchor)                  |
| Space 2  | A₄                               |
| Line 3   | B₄                               |
| Space 3  | C₅                               |
| Line 4   | D₅                               |
| Space 4  | E₅                               |
| Line 5   | **F₅**                           |

### The Bass Clef (F Clef)  

The **bass clef** places a stylized “F” over the fourth line from the bottom. That line is **F₃** (the F below middle C). The surrounding pitches follow the same stepwise pattern:

| Position | Pitch |
|----------|-------|
| Line 1   | **G₂** |
| Space 1  | A₂    |
| Line 2   | B₂    |
| Space 2  | **C₃** |
| Line 3   | D₃    |
| Space 3  | E₃    |
| Line 4   | **F₃** (anchor) |
| Space 4  | G₃    |
| Line 5   | A₃    |

*Tip:* Memorize the “Every Good Boy Does Fine” (E‑G‑B‑D‑F) mnemonic for treble **lines**, and “FACE” for treble **spaces**. For bass, use “Good Boys Do Fine Always” (G‑B‑D‑F‑A) for lines and “All Cows Eat Grass” (A‑C‑E‑G) for spaces.

---

## Note Values and Their Rests  

### Whole, Half, Quarter, Eighth, and Sixteenth  

Rhythm is expressed through **note heads**, **stems**, and **flags** (or beams). The following table pairs each note value with its visual components and relative duration:

| Symbol | Stem? | Flag(s) / Beam | Duration (relative to a whole note) |
|--------|-------|----------------|--------------------------------------|
| **Whole note** | No | — | 4 beats (in 4/4) |
| **Half note** | Yes | — | 2 beats |
| **Quarter note** | Yes | — | 1 beat |
| **Eighth note** | Yes | One flag (or beamed) | ½ beat |
| **Sixteenth note** | Yes | Two flags (or beamed) | ¼ beat |

### Corresponding Rests  

Every note value has a matching **rest**, a symbol indicating silence for the same amount of time.

| Rest Symbol | Duration (relative to a whole note) |
|-------------|--------------------------------------|
| Whole rest | 4 beats |
| Half rest | 2 beats |
| Quarter rest | 1 beat |
| Eighth rest | ½ beat |
| Sixteenth rest | ¼ beat |

The **placement** of a rest on the staff does not affect its duration; rests are centered horizontally between the staff lines.

### Visual Relationships  

- **Stem direction:** Stems point **upward** when the note head is on or below the middle line; they point **downward** when the note head sits on or above the middle line. This convention keeps the notation compact.
- **Beaming:** Eighth‑ and sixteenth‑note stems are often **beamed** together in groups of two or four, clarifying rhythmic grouping.
- **Flag orientation:** Single flags curve opposite the stem direction; double‑flag notes have two stacked curves.

---

## Putting Rhythm on the Staff  

Consider the following measure in 4/4 time, written in treble clef:

```
𝅝 ──𝅗𝅥────𝅘𝅥────𝅘𝅥𝅮──𝅘𝅥𝅯──𝅘𝅥𝅰──𝅘𝅥𝅲
```

(Visually: a whole note, a half note, a quarter note, an eighth note, and a sixteenth note.)

- **Beat allocation:** The whole note occupies the entire measure (4 beats). The half note takes 2 beats, the quarter 1 beat, the eighth ½ beat, and the sixteenth ¼ beat. Adding them together (4 + 2 + 1 + ½ + ¼) exceeds a 4‑beat measure, so this example illustrates how note values stack across **multiple measures**.  

When writing a simple melody, you’ll often combine these values to fill exactly the number of beats dictated by the **time signature** (e.g., 4/4, 3/4, 6/8).  

**Exercise:** Sketch a 4/4 measure that uses one half note, two quarter notes, and two eighth notes. Verify that the total adds to four beats.

---

## Accidentals: Sharps, Flats, and Naturals  

### The Three Core Accidentals  

- **Sharp (♯):** Raises the pitch **one semitone** (half step).  
- **Flat (♭):** Lowers the pitch **one semitone**.  
- **Natural (♮):** Cancels any previous accidental for that pitch within the same **measure**.  

Accidentals are placed **immediately to the left of the note head**. Their effect persists for the remainder of the measure for that **specific staff position** (i.e., same line or space, regardless of octave). When the measure ends, the accidental effect is cleared.

### Contextual Example  

```
Measure 1 (Treble):
   ♯  ♭  ♮
   G   A   G
```

- The first G is sharpened to **G♯**.  
- The A is flattened to **A♭**.  
- The second G carries a natural sign, returning it to **G** (not G♯).  

If a **different G** (e.g., an octave higher) appears later in the same measure without an accidental, it **inherits** the previous accidental (G♯) because the rule applies to the *staff position*, not the specific octave.

### Using Accidentals with Ledger Lines  

When a melody climbs beyond the five lines, **ledger lines** extend the staff. Accidentals function identically on ledger lines:

```
... (ledger line) ... ♯  (note on ledger line)
```

The sharp still raises that pitch by a semitone, regardless of its vertical distance from the main staff.

---

## Ledger Lines: Extending the Staff  

### What Are Ledger Lines?  

Ledger lines are **short, horizontal strokes** added above or below the staff to represent pitches outside the normal range. Each ledger line essentially becomes an extension of the staff, allowing you to read notes as if the staff continued indefinitely.

### Practical Guidelines  

- **Spacing:** Ledger lines are spaced exactly like the staff lines—maintaining the same vertical distance.  
- **Reading:** Treat a note on a ledger line as you would any line within the staff. Apply the same clef anchor point to determine its pitch.  
- **Accidentals:** Place accidentals directly to the left of the note head, even if the head sits on a ledger line.  

### Example Melody  

Below is a short treble‑clef melody that uses ledger lines and accidentals. (In text, ledger lines are represented by dashes.)

```
Measure 1 (4/4):
   (E₅)  -♭-  (D₅)  -♯-  (C₅)  (B₄)  (A₄)

Notation (simplified):
   ──────♭───♯─────
   o     o     o   o
   |_____|_____|____|
   (ledger)          (no ledger)
```

- **E₅** sits on the top line of the treble staff.  
- **D₅** is placed on a **ledger line** just above the top line, with a flat sign, making it **D♭₅**.  
- **C₅** sits on the space just below the top line, with a sharp, becoming **C♯₅**.  

The melody spans from middle C (C₄) up to D♭₅, illustrating how ledger lines and accidentals combine to cover a broader pitch range.

---

## Reading and Writing Simple Melodies  

### Step‑by‑Step Approach  

1. **Identify the clef** – Determine whether you’re working in treble or bass.  
2. **Locate the anchor line** (G₄ for treble, F₃ for bass).  
3. **Count lines and spaces** from the anchor to find the pitch name.  
4. **Check for accidentals** – Apply any sharp, flat, or natural signs that appear to the left of the note head.  
5. **Determine duration** – Look at the note head, stem, and flags (or beams) to assign the appropriate rhythmic value.  
6. **Add rests** where silence is indicated.  
7. **Write the note** – If you’re composing, place the note head on the correct line/space, add stems/flags, and include any needed accidentals. Use ledger lines when the pitch lies outside the staff.

### Practice Prompt  

> Write a two‑measure melody in **bass clef** using the following constraints:  
> - Time signature: **3/4**  
> - Note values: one half note, two quarter notes, one eighth note, and one sixteenth note.  
> - Include at least one **flat** and one **natural** accidental, and a note that requires a **ledger line**.  

*Solution outline (not provided here)*: Start with a half note on the fourth line (F₃), add a flat on the second space (A♭₂), place a natural on the ledger line below the staff (E♮₂), and finish with the eighth and sixteenth notes on the first line and space, respectively.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Quick Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----------|
| **Confusing treble and bass lines** | Relying on visual similarity rather than clef symbols. | **Always locate the clef first**; then count from its anchor. |
| **Forgetting that accidentals reset each measure** | Assuming a sharp or flat applies for the whole piece. | **Mark the measure boundary** mentally; after the bar line, start fresh. |
| **Misreading ledger‑line notes as spaces** | Ledger lines can be faint or crowded. | **Count ledger lines** just like staff lines; treat them as extensions. |
| **Applying a natural to the wrong pitch** | Natural signs cancel *any* previous accidental for that staff position, not just the immediate one. | **Identify the exact line/space** the natural sits on; only that pitch is affected. |
| **Over‑beaming eighth‑note groups** | Grouping notes without considering the underlying beat structure. | **Group beams** according to the **time signature** (e.g., in 4/4, beam eighth notes in groups of two). |

---

## Applying the Concepts: From Sight‑Reading to Notation  

When you encounter a new piece, follow this rapid checklist:

1. **Glance at the clef** – treble or bass?  
2. **Spot any key signature** (though not covered here, it will appear later).  
3. **Read the first measure**: locate each note’s line/space, apply accidentals, note duration, and rest symbols.  
4. **Tap the rhythm**: count beats aloud (“1‑2‑3‑4…”), aligning each note value with the beat.  
5. **Play or sing** the pitches, confirming they match the written staff positions.  

Conversely, when you **write** a melody:

- Begin with a **clear rhythmic skeleton** (e.g., “half‑quarter‑eighth‑sixteenth”).  
- Place **note heads** on the desired lines/spaces, adding accidentals as needed.  
- Use **ledger lines** for any pitches beyond the five‑line range.  
- Double‑check that the total duration matches the chosen **time signature**.

---

## Bridging to the Next Chapter  

Having internalized the visual grammar of the staff, you’re now ready to explore **scales and key signatures**, where the pattern of whole‑ and half‑steps builds the tonal framework for the melodies you just learned to read and write.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- The **staff** consists of five lines and four spaces; **clefs** assign a specific pitch to one of those lines (G₄ for treble, F₃ for bass).  
- **Line and space names** follow predictable sequences; mnemonics (“EGBDF”, “FACE”, etc.) aid memorization.  
- **Note values** (whole, half, quarter, eighth, sixteenth) and their matching **rests** define rhythmic duration; stems, flags, and beams convey these values visually.  
- **Accidentals**—sharp (♯), flat (♭), natural (♮)—alter a pitch by a semitone and apply only within the current measure for that staff position.  
- **Ledger lines** extend the staff upward or downward, allowing notes beyond the five‑line range; accidentals work the same way on ledger lines.  
- Effective sight‑reading and notation require a systematic approach: identify clef → locate anchor → count lines/spaces → apply accidentals → determine duration.  
- Common errors include confusing clefs, ignoring measure‑resetting of accidentals, and misreading ledger‑line positions; a quick mental checklist prevents these slips.  

With these fundamentals mastered, you can confidently translate any simple melody from page to instrument and back again.

## From “What’s This Note?” to “Why Does This Piece Feel So Familiar”

Imagine you’re sitting at a piano, a friend hands you a lead sheet that reads **“C major”** at the top. You glance at the staff, see a handful of sharps, and instinctively know the piece will sound bright, open, and “home‑like.” A few measures later the chord changes to **A minor**—the same key signature, but a different emotional color.  
How did you know that A minor shares the same accidentals as C major? How did you instantly recognize the pattern of whole‑steps and half‑steps that defines each scale?  

The ability to **construct major and natural minor scales**, **read and write key signatures**, and **navigate the circle of fifths** turns a collection of notes into a coherent tonal landscape. This chapter gives you the tools to do exactly that.

---

## 1. Building Scales from Whole‑Step / Half‑Step Patterns  

### 1.1 The Major Scale Formula  

A major scale is defined by the repeating pattern of whole steps (W) and half steps (H):

```
W – W – H – W – W – W – H
```

A **whole step** equals two semitones (e.g., C → D), while a **half step** equals one semitone (e.g., E → F). Starting from any tonic pitch, apply the pattern to generate the seven distinct scale degrees, then return to the tonic an octave higher.

**Example: C major**  

1. Start on C.  
2. W → D  
3. W → E  
4. H → F  
5. W → G  
6. W → A  
7. W → B  
8. H → C (octave)

The result is the familiar C‑major diatonic series: C D E F G A B C.

### 1.2 The Natural Minor Scale Formula  

The natural minor (also called the Aeolian mode) follows a different pattern:

```
W – H – W – W – H – W – W
```

**Example: A natural minor** (relative minor of C major)

1. Start on A.  
2. W → B  
3. H → C  
4. W → D  
5. W → E  
6. H → F  
7. W → G  
8. W → A (octave)

Result: A B C D E F G A. Notice that the accidentals are exactly the same as those of C major—no sharps or flats appear.

### 1.3 Quick‑Reference Construction Checklist  

When you need to write a scale on the spot:

1. **Identify the tonic** (the note that gives the scale its name).  
2. **Choose the pattern** (major or natural minor).  
3. **Apply the W/H sequence** step by step, counting semitones on the staff.  
4. **Add the octave** to complete the eight‑note series.  
5. **Check for accidentals**: any note that falls outside the natural letters A–G will require a sharp (♯) or flat (♭) sign.

Practice this process in all 12 pitch classes; the patterns never change, only the starting point does.

---

## 2. From Scales to Key Signatures  

A **key signature** tells you, at a glance, which notes are consistently sharpened or flattened throughout a piece. It is derived directly from the scale’s accidentals.

### 2.1 Deriving a Major‑Key Signature  

1. **Write the major scale** using the W‑W‑H‑W‑W‑W‑H pattern.  
2. **Mark any notes that are not natural** (i.e., that require a ♯ or ♭).  
3. **Collect those accidentals** and place them at the beginning of each staff line/space, in the order prescribed by the circle of fifths (see §3).  

**Example: G major**  

- Scale: G A B C D E F♯ G  
- Accidentals: only F♯.  
- Key signature: a single sharp on the F line (the fifth line of the treble clef).

### 2.2 Deriving a Natural‑Minor Key Signature  

The natural minor shares its key signature with its **relative major** (the major key whose tonic is a minor third above). Therefore, you can:

- **Find the relative major** (up a minor third) and copy its key signature, **or**  
- **Build the natural minor scale** and collect its accidentals directly.

**Example: E minor**  

- Relative major: G major (one sharp).  
- Natural‑minor scale: E F♯ G A B C D E → accidentals: F♯ only.  
- Key signature: same single sharp as G major.

### 2.3 Accidentals Inside a Key  

Even with a key signature in place, composers may write **non‑diatonic accidentals** (e.g., a G♯ in C major). These are:

- **Temporary**: they affect only the measure (or the single note) unless a natural sign cancels them.  
- **Indicative of modulation or chromaticism**: a clue that the music is moving toward a new tonal center.

When you see an accidental that **does not belong to the key signature**, treat it as a **color tone** or a **pivot** for a modulation. Recognizing this distinction is essential for accurate sight‑reading and analysis.

---

## 3. The Circle of Fifths: A Roadmap for Keys  

The **circle of fifths** arranges the twelve pitch classes in a clockwise order of perfect fifths (C–G–D–A–E–B–F♯–C♯–G♯–D♯–A♯–E♭–B♭–F–C). Two concentric rings display the order of sharps (clockwise) and flats (counter‑clockwise).  

### 3.1 Ordering Sharps and Flats  

- **Sharps** appear in the order: **F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯, A♯, E♯, B♯**.  
- **Flats** appear in the order: **B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭, C♭, F♭**.  

Each step clockwise adds a sharp; each step counter‑clockwise adds a flat.

**Visual cue**: The key signature for a given major key can be read directly from the circle. For example, the key of D major sits two steps clockwise from C, thus has **two sharps** (F♯ and C♯).

### 3.2 Finding Relative Majors and Minors  

- **Relative major**: move **up a minor third** (three semitones) from the minor tonic.  
- **Relative minor**: move **down a minor third** from the major tonic.

Because the circle is built on fifths, the relative minor of any major key lies **directly opposite** on the circle.

| Major | Key Sig. | Relative Minor | Key Sig. |
|-------|----------|----------------|----------|
| C     | 0♯/0♭    | A              | 0♯/0♭    |
| G     | 1♯       | E              | 1♯       |
| D     | 2♯       | B              | 2♯       |
| A     | 3♯       | F♯             | 3♯       |
| E     | 4♯       | C♯             | 4♯       |
| B/F♯  | 5♯/6♭    | G♯/D♭          | 5♯/6♭    |
| …     | …        | …              | …        |

*(The table continues around the circle; you can construct the full list yourself.)*

### 3.3 Closely Related Keys and Common Modulations  

Keys that sit **adjacent** on the circle share all but one accidental. This makes them ideal for smooth modulations because the transition requires only a single accidental change.

- **From C major (0♯) to G major (1♯)**: add F♯.  
- **From A minor (0♯) to E minor (1♯)**: add F♯.  

**Common modulation pattern**:  
1. **Pivot chord** – a chord that belongs to both the original and destination key.  
2. **Introduce the new accidental** via that chord, then resolve to the new tonic.

*Example*: In a piece in C major, the chord **E minor** (E‑G‑B) can serve as a pivot because it also functions as the **iii** chord in C major and the **i** chord in E minor. When the music moves from C major to E minor, the new accidental (F♯) appears first in the **E minor** chord (as the leading tone to G), then the piece settles into the new key.

---

## 4. Applying the Concepts: A Real‑World Scenario  

### 4.1 Scenario: Preparing for a Band Rehearsal  

You are the keyboardist for a four‑piece pop band. The setlist includes three songs:

1. **“Sunrise”** – marked **D major**.  
2. **“Midnight Walk”** – marked **B minor**.  
3. **“Finale”** – marked **G major**, but the bridge hints at **E minor**.

Your tasks:

- **Write out the scales** you’ll need for improvisation.  
- **Identify the key signatures** so you can set up the appropriate pedalboard accidentals.  
- **Plan smooth transitions** between songs.

#### Step‑by‑Step

1. **Determine key signatures** using the circle of fifths.  
   - D major: two sharps (F♯, C♯).  
   - B minor: relative minor of D major → same two sharps.  
   - G major: one sharp (F♯).  
   - E minor: relative minor of G major → same one sharp.

2. **Construct the scales**.  
   - D major: D E F♯ G A B C♯ D.  
   - B natural minor: B C♯ D E F♯ G A B.  
   - G major: G A B C D E F♯ G.  
   - E natural minor: E F♯ G A B C D E.

3. **Plan the bridge modulation** (G → E minor).  
   - Use a **pivot chord** such as **B minor** (B‑D‑F♯), which is **iii** in G major and **v** in E minor.  
   - Introduce the new key by adding the **C♯** accidental (present in the B minor chord) and resolve to **E minor**.

4. **Set pedalboard**: program one preset with two sharps, another with one sharp, and a third with “no accidentals” for any potential chromatic passages.

By following the systematic approach outlined above, you move from merely reading the printed key signatures to **actively shaping** the harmonic flow of the performance.

---

## 5. Practice Tools and Tips  

### 5.1 Quick‑Lookup Cheat Sheet  

| # of Sharps | Keys (Major) | Relative Minor |
|-------------|--------------|----------------|
| 0           | C            | A              |
| 1           | G            | E              |
| 2           | D            | B              |
| 3           | A            | F♯             |
| 4           | E            | C♯             |
| 5           | B / C♭       | G♯ / A♭        |
| 6           | F♯ / G♭      | D♯ / E♭        |
| 7           | C♯ / D♭      | A♯ / B♭        |

*For flats, read the table from right to left (e.g., 3 flats = A♭ major, relative minor = F minor).*

### 5.2 Mnemonic Devices  

- **Sharps order**: “**F**ather **C**ould **G**et **D**runk **A**t **E**very **B**ar.”  
- **Flats order**: “**B**ad **E**lephants **A**re **D**angerously **G**alloping **C**razy **F**oxes.”  

These sentences help you recall the exact sequence of accidentals when constructing key signatures.

### 5.3 Exercise Routine  

1. **Scale Generation** – Pick a random tonic, write the major and natural minor scales, and list the accidentals.  
2. **Key Signature Matching** – Using the cheat sheet, verify that the accidentals you listed correspond to the correct key signature.  
3. **Circle Navigation** – Starting from C, move clockwise three steps; name the key, its key signature, and its relative minor. Then move counter‑clockwise two steps and repeat.  
4. **Modulation Sketch** – Choose two adjacent keys on the circle, write a four‑measure progression that uses a pivot chord, and notate the accidental change in the staff.

Consistent daily work on these drills will cement the patterns in muscle memory, making scale construction and key recognition automatic.

---

## 6. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Remedy |
|---------|----------------|--------|
| **Confusing relative majors/minors** | Remembering “a minor third up” but applying it to the wrong direction. | Visualize the circle: the relative minor sits **directly opposite** the major key. |
| **Adding accidentals in the wrong order** | Memorizing the sharp/flat sequences but forgetting the clockwise/counter‑clockwise rule. | Always **refer to the circle** first; then apply the appropriate order. |
| **Assuming every minor key uses the natural minor pattern** | Natural minor omits the raised seventh that appears in harmonic/minor forms. | Keep this chapter’s focus on **natural minor only**; treat harmonic/minor later. |
| **Writing a key signature with duplicate accidentals** | Accidentals placed on the wrong line/space, especially in the bass clef. | Use the staff knowledge from the earlier chapter: locate each accidental on its correct line or space before moving to the next. |
| **Neglecting the effect of accidentals within a measure** | Forgetting that an accidental lasts for the rest of the measure unless canceled. | After sight‑reading a measure with a non‑key accidental, **mark** it mentally (or with a small underline) until the bar line. |

---

## 7. From Theory to Performance  

When you sit down to play, the scale patterns and key signatures become **road signs** guiding your improvisation, phrasing, and chord choices. A solid grasp of these fundamentals lets you:

- **Anticipate chord tones** when improvising over a progression.  
- **Spot‑read confidently** because you instantly know which notes are “in‑key.”  
- **Create purposeful modulations** that feel natural to the listener, rather than abrupt key jumps.

The next chapter will build on this foundation by exploring **intervals**—the distances that connect the scale degrees you’ve just mapped out. Mastering intervals will give you the vocabulary to describe why a particular note “sounds right” over a given chord.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Major and natural minor scales** are built from fixed whole‑step/half‑step patterns (W‑W‑H‑W‑W‑W‑H for major; W‑H‑W‑W‑H‑W‑W for natural minor).  
- **Key signatures** are derived directly from the accidentals present in a scale; the major key’s signature is shared by its relative natural minor.  
- The **circle of fifths** orders keys by adding sharps clockwise or flats counter‑clockwise, provides a quick lookup for key signatures, and reveals relative majors/minors.  
- **Relative majors/minors** sit opposite each other on the circle; move up a minor third from a minor tonic to find its relative major, and down a minor third from a major tonic to find its relative minor.  
- **Closely related keys** (adjacent on the circle) differ by only one accidental, making them ideal for smooth modulations using pivot chords.  
- **Accidentals outside the key signature** are temporary, indicating chromaticism or a modulation; they do not alter the underlying key signature unless the piece formally changes key.  
- Practical tools—cheat sheets, mnemonics, and targeted exercises—help internalize these patterns for fast, reliable application in performance and analysis.

modules.title: Intervals and Their Functions
modules.content:
## From a Single Note to a Musical Sentence  

Imagine you’re sitting at a piano and you hear a lone **C** ringing. Within a heartbeat you can imagine it “talking” to another note—perhaps a **G** that feels stable, or a **B♭** that creates tension begging for release. Those relationships are the backbone of every melody, harmony, and improvisation you’ll ever write. In this chapter we turn that intuition into precise language: the names, qualities, and functions of intervals.

---

## 1. Naming the Distance – From Unison to Octave and Beyond  

### 1.1 Simple Intervals  

A **simple interval** spans eight diatonic steps or fewer (unison → octave). The distance is counted by letter names, not by semitones:

| Simple Interval | Example (C as root) | Number of Letter Steps |
|----------------|---------------------|------------------------|
| Unison (P1)    | C – C               | 1 (C to C)             |
| Second (2)     | C – D               | 2 (C → D)              |
| Third (3)      | C – E               | 3 (C → D → E)          |
| Fourth (4)     | C – F               | 4 (C → D → E → F)      |
| Fifth (5)      | C – G               | 5 (C → D → E → F → G)  |
| Sixth (6)      | C – A               | 6 (C → D → E → F → G → A) |
| Seventh (7)    | C – B               | 7 (C → D → E → F → G → A → B) |
| Octave (P8)    | C – C′              | 8 (C → D → … → B → C′) |

> **Tip:** When you count, include both the starting and ending notes. “C to E” is a **third**, not a “second”.

### 1.2 Compound Intervals  

When the distance exceeds an octave, we add the appropriate simple interval to an octave. The naming convention simply prefixes the simple interval number with the next octave number:

| Compound Interval | Example (C as root) | How it’s built |
|-------------------|---------------------|----------------|
| Ninth (9)         | C – D′              | Octave (8) + Second (2) |
| Tenth (10)        | C – E′              | Octave + Third |
| Eleventh (11)     | C – F′              | Octave + Fourth |
| Twelfth (12)      | C – G′              | Octave + Fifth |
| Thirteenth (13)   | C – A′              | Octave + Sixth |
| Fourteenth (14)   | C – B′              | Octave + Seventh |
| Double Octave (15) | C – C″             | Two octaves |

In practice, composers often think of a **ninth** as “an octave plus a second,” but the interval name (ninth) conveys both the span and its functional role (e.g., a “dominant ninth” chord).

---

## 2. Interval Quality – Perfect, Major, Minor, Augmented, Diminished  

### 2.1 The Perfect Family  

Unisons, fourths, fifths, and octaves belong to the **perfect** family because their acoustic ratios are especially stable (e.g., 2:1 for the octave, 3:2 for the perfect fifth). Their qualities are:

| Interval | Perfect | Augmented | Diminished |
|----------|---------|-----------|------------|
| Unison   | P1      | A1 (♯1)   | d1 (♭♭1)   |
| Fourth   | P4      | A4 (♯4)   | d4 (♭4)    |
| Fifth    | P5      | A5 (♯5)   | d5 (♭5)    |
| Octave   | P8      | A8 (♯8)   | d8 (♭♭8)   |

*An augmented perfect interval raises the pitch by one semitone; a diminished perfect lowers it by one semitone.*

### 2.2 The Major/Minor Family  

Seconds, thirds, sixths, and sevenths belong to the **major/minor** family. Their qualities are:

| Interval | Major | Minor | Augmented | Diminished |
|----------|-------|-------|-----------|------------|
| Second   | M2 (whole step) | m2 (semitone) | A2 (♯2) | d2 (♭♭2) |
| Third    | M3 (four semitones) | m3 (three) | A3 (♯3) | d3 (♭♭3) |
| Sixth    | M6 (nine) | m6 (eight) | A6 (♯6) | d6 (♭♭6) |
| Seventh  | M7 (eleven) | m7 (ten) | A7 (♯7) | d7 (♭♭7) |

**Key point:** The **major** form is the “default” distance within the diatonic major scale; the **minor** form is a single semitone smaller. Augmented and diminished versions are built by adding or subtracting a semitone from the major/minor forms, respectively.

### 2.3 Quick Reference Cheat Sheet  

- **P** = Perfect (unison, 4th, 5th, octave)  
- **M** = Major (2, 3, 6, 7)  
- **m** = Minor (2, 3, 6, 7)  
- **A** = Augmented (one semitone larger than perfect or major)  
- **d** = Diminished (one semitone smaller than perfect or minor)  

When you see “A4” read it as “augmented fourth” (often called a **tritone**).

---

## 3. Consonance, Dissonance, and Their Resolutions  

### 3.1 The Two Families  

| Consonant Intervals (stable) | Dissonant Intervals (unstable) |
|------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Unison (P1)                  | Minor second (m2) |
| Octave (P8)                  | Major second (M2) |
| Perfect fifth (P5)           | Minor seventh (m7) |
| Perfect fourth (P4) – *sometimes* | Major seventh (M7) |
| Major third (M3)             | Tritone (A4/d5) |
| Minor third (m3)             | Augmented second (A2) |
| Minor sixth (m6)             | Diminished fifth (d5) |
| Major sixth (M6)             | Augmented sixth (A6) |
| Major seventh (M7) – *often* | — |

*Why the ambiguity?* In tonal harmony the perfect fourth is consonant when it resolves to a third (e.g., in a cadential 4‑3 suspension) but can function as a dissonance in other contexts. For the purpose of this chapter we treat the perfect fourth as **conditionally consonant**.

### 3.2 Typical Resolutions  

| Dissonant Interval | Common Resolution Direction | Example (C as root) |
|--------------------|-----------------------------|---------------------|
| m2 (C–D♭)           | **Stepwise** upward to a major third (E) or downward to a perfect unison (C) | C–D♭ → C–E |
| M2 (C–D)            | **Stepwise** down to a perfect unison or up to a minor third | C–D → C–E♭ |
| Tritone (A4/d5, C–F♯) | **Contrary motion** to a perfect fifth (G) or perfect fourth (F) | C–F♯ → C–G |
| m7 (C–B♭)           | **Downward** by step to the octave (C) or upward to a perfect fifth (G) | C–B♭ → C–C′ |
| M7 (C–B)            | **Downward** by half step to the octave (C) | C–B → C–C′ |

**Resolution principle:** Dissonant intervals tend to move by the smallest possible melodic step (often a half or whole step) toward a consonant interval. This “tension‑and‑release” pattern is the engine of Western tonal music.

### 3.3 Applying Consonance/Dissonance in Melody  

When crafting a melodic line, keep the following heuristic in mind:

1. **Stepwise motion** (seconds) is the default—most melodies consist of mostly consonant intervals (unisons, thirds, sixths) broken up by occasional leaps.
2. **Leaps larger than a fifth** are usually followed by a step in the opposite direction to smooth the line.
3. **Tritones** rarely appear as isolated melodic intervals; they tend to be part of a harmonic context (e.g., a dominant seventh chord) or resolved quickly.

---

## 4. Building Chords and Melodic Lines from Intervals  

### 4.1 Stacking Intervals to Form Triads (Preview for Chapter 4)  

Even though full triad construction belongs to the next chapter, understanding that a **triad** is simply a stack of two thirds (a third on top of another third) helps you see why interval quality matters:

- **Major triad:** Root → **M3** → **m3** (e.g., C‑E‑G)  
- **Minor triad:** Root → **m3** → **M3** (e.g., C‑E♭‑G)  

When you hear a chord, you can mentally “unpack” it into its constituent intervals and instantly recognize its function.

### 4.2 Using Intervals to Sketch a Melody  

**Scenario:** You are writing a simple 8‑measure melody over a I–V–vi–IV progression in C major (C – G – Am – F). Your goal is to emphasize the tonic (C) on the downbeats while creating forward motion.

1. **Identify the chord tones** (root, third, fifth) for each harmony.  
   - I (C): C, E, G  
   - V (G): G, B, D  
   - vi (Am): A, C, E  
   - IV (F): F, A, C  

2. **Choose intervals** that connect these tones:  
   - From **C** (downbeat of measure 1) jump a **M6** up to **A** (the sixth of the tonic, also the third of vi).  
   - Resolve the **M6** by stepping down a **m2** to **G** (the fifth of I).  
   - On the V chord, move from **G** up a **M3** to **B** (the third of V).  
   - Use a **P4** (tritone) from **B** to **F** (the fourth of the IV chord) and resolve it down a **m2** to **E** (the third of vi).  

3. **Check consonance**: Each leap (M6, M3, P4) lands on a chord tone, giving a sense of stability despite the large intervals. The subsequent stepwise motions (m2) provide the needed resolution.

**Resulting interval sequence:** P1 – M6 – m2 – M3 – P4 – m2 … This pattern illustrates how you can deliberately mix **consonant** and **dissonant** intervals to shape a melodic contour while staying grounded in the underlying harmony.

### 4.3 Interval Recognition for Improvisation  

When improvising, treat each scale degree as a **source of intervals** you can draw from:

| Scale Degree | Common Interval Options (relative to tonic) |
|--------------|---------------------------------------------|
| 1 (tonic)    | P1, m2, M2, m3, M3, P4, A4/d5, P5, m6, M6, m7, M7 |
| 2 (supertonic) | m2, M2, m3, M3, P4, A4/d5 |
| 3 (mediant)   | m3, M3, P4, A4/d5, P5 |
| …            | … (continue similarly) |

By internalizing which intervals are **diatonic** (fit the key) versus **chromatic** (outside the key), you can instantly decide whether a note will sound **consonant** or create a **tension** that needs to resolve.

---

## 5. Practical Exercises  

### 5.1 Interval Identification Drill  

1. Write a **C major scale** on the staff (refer to the earlier chapter on scales).  
2. Randomly select two notes and label the interval **both by number and quality** (e.g., “M6”).  
3. Check your answer using a piano or a digital tuner.  

Repeat until you can name any simple interval within a second.

### 5.2 Building a Mini‑Phrase  

- Choose a **root note** (C).  
- Construct a four‑note phrase using the following interval pattern: **P1 – M3 – P5 – m2**.  
- Notate the phrase on the treble clef staff, then sing it, paying attention to the tension created by the final **m2**.

### 5.3 Consonance‑Resolution Mapping  

Take a short chord progression (e.g., I–IV–V–I). For each chord change, write down the **interval** between the **top voice** of the first chord and the **top voice** of the next chord. Classify each interval as consonant or dissonant and note the **resolution direction** (up/down). This exercise highlights how voice leading naturally respects interval function.

---

## 6. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| **Confusing “major” with “perfect.”** | Both use the letter “M” in shorthand. | Remember: **perfect** applies only to unisons, 4ths, 5ths, and octaves. |
| **Calling a diminished fifth a “tritone” without context.** | The term “tritone” is often used for both A4 and d5, but they differ enharmonically. | Specify the spelling (e.g., **A4** = F♯, **d5** = B♭) when discussing resolution. |
| **Assuming every leap must resolve downward.** | Direction of resolution depends on the interval’s harmonic role, not just its size. | Examine the surrounding harmony: a **M6** may resolve upward to a seventh or downward to a third. |
| **Overusing augmented intervals in a diatonic melody.** | Augmented intervals are inherently dissonant and demand resolution. | Reserve augmented intervals for moments of heightened tension (e.g., leading‑tone resolution). |

---

## 7. Connecting Intervals to the Bigger Picture  

You’ve already mastered **pitch notation** and **scale construction**. Intervals are the bridge that turns static notes into dynamic relationships. The next chapter will show you how stacking these relationships creates **triads** and **seventh chords**, but the groundwork you lay here—recognizing interval names, qualities, and functions—will make that transition seamless.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Simple vs. compound:** Simple intervals cover unison to octave; compound intervals add an octave to a simple interval (e.g., ninth = octave + second).  
- **Quality families:** Perfect (P1, P4, P5, P8) and major/minor (2, 3, 6, 7) each have augmented and diminished forms.  
- **Consonance & dissonance:** Consonant intervals are stable; dissonant intervals create tension that resolves by the smallest possible step toward a consonance.  
- **Functional use:** Identify intervals in a melody to shape tension‑and‑release; stack intervals (especially thirds) to form chords; employ interval awareness in improvisation to stay within or deliberately step outside the key.  
- **Practical habit:** Regularly name intervals on the staff, listen for their acoustic character, and experiment with resolution patterns. Mastery of intervals turns every note you see on the staff into a purposeful musical decision.

modules.title: Triads and Seventh Chords
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Hook: The Turnaround That Won a Hit

Imagine you’re sitting at a jam session. The bassist drops a **ii–V–I** progression in the key of G major, and the guitarist immediately adds color by turning each triad into a seventh chord. Within two bars the groove feels richer, the tension and release become palpable, and the audience leans in. That extra emotional pull comes from the **seventh chords** built on the same roots you just learned to stack as triads. Mastering how to build those chords from any root—and how to move them fluidly into any key—gives you the same tool that turned a simple three‑chord loop into a chart‑topping hook.

Below we unpack the construction, labeling, and transposition of the four essential triads and the four foundational seventh chords. The patterns rely on the interval knowledge you already explored in *Intervals and Their Functions*; you’ll see how those intervals become the scaffolding for harmony.

---

## 1. Constructing the Four Basic Triads

A **triad** is a three‑note stack built in thirds from a root. The quality of the triad depends on the specific intervals between the root, third, and fifth. Using the interval formulas from the previous chapter, you can generate any triad in any key.

| Triad Type | Interval Formula (Root → 3rd → 5th) | Example: C‑root |
|------------|--------------------------------------|-----------------|
| **Major** | **M3 – P5** | C – E (M3) – G (P5) |
| **Minor** | **m3 – P5** | C – Eb (m3) – G (P5) |
| **Diminished** | **m3 – d5** | C – Eb (m3) – Gb (d5) |
| **Augmented** | **M3 – A5** | C – E (M3) – G♯ (A5) |

### 1.1 Step‑by‑Step Construction

1. **Choose a root** (any pitch you see on the staff or think of on your instrument).  
2. **Add the third** using the appropriate major or minor third interval.  
3. **Add the fifth** using the perfect, diminished, or augmented fifth as required.

> **Tip:** Write the intervals as a sequence of half‑steps:  
> • Major triad = 4 h + 3 h (M3 = 4 h, P5 = 7 h total)  
> • Minor triad = 3 h + 4 h (m3 = 3 h, P5 = 7 h total)  
> • Diminished triad = 3 h + 3 h (m3 + d5 = 6 h total)  
> • Augmented triad = 4 h + 4 h (M3 + A5 = 8 h total)

### 1.2 Triad Construction in Any Key (Example: F♯)

| Triad | Intervals (half‑steps) | Notes |
|-------|------------------------|-------|
| **Major** | 4 h → 3 h | F♯ – A♯ – C♯ |
| **Minor** | 3 h → 4 h | F♯ – A – C♯ |
| **Diminished** | 3 h → 3 h | F♯ – A – C |
| **Augmented** | 4 h → 4 h | F♯ – A♯ – D |

By memorizing the half‑step patterns, you can write any triad without consulting a chart.

---

## 2. Building the Four Fundamental Seventh Chords

A **seventh chord** adds a fourth note—a seventh above the root—to a triad. The quality of the seventh (major or minor) combined with the triad quality defines the chord type. The four seventh chords that appear most often in tonal music are:

| Seventh Chord | Triad Basis | Seventh Interval |
|---------------|------------|-------------------|
| **Dominant 7** | Major | **m7** (minor seventh) |
| **Major 7** | Major | **M7** (major seventh) |
| **Minor 7** | Minor | **m7** |
| **Half‑Diminished 7** (also called **m7♭5**) | Diminished | **m7** |

### 2.1 Interval Formulas

| Chord | Formula (Root → 3rd → 5th → 7th) |
|-------|----------------------------------|
| **Dominant 7** | **M3 – P5 – m7** |
| **Major 7** | **M3 – P5 – M7** |
| **Minor 7** | **m3 – P5 – m7** |
| **Half‑Diminished 7** | **m3 – d5 – m7** |

### 2.2 Constructing Each Seventh Chord (Step‑by‑Step)

1. **Build the underlying triad** using the method from Section 1.  
2. **Add the seventh** on top of the fifth, respecting the interval listed above.  

#### Example: G‑root Dominant 7

1. Major triad: G – B – D (M3, P5).  
2. Add a **minor seventh** (10 h above G): F.  
3. Result: **G⁷** = G – B – D – F.

#### Example: B♭‑root Half‑Diminished 7

1. Diminished triad: B♭ – Db – Fb (enharmonically E).  
2. Add a **minor seventh** (10 h above B♭): **Ab**.  
3. Result: **B♭m7♭5** = B♭ – Db – Fb – Ab.

### 2.3 Quick Reference Chart (Half‑Step Distances)

| Chord | Root → 3rd | 3rd → 5th | 5th → 7th |
|-------|------------|----------|----------|
| **Dominant 7** | 4 h | 3 h | 3 h |
| **Major 7** | 4 h | 3 h | 4 h |
| **Minor 7** | 3 h | 4 h | 3 h |
| **Half‑Diminished 7** | 3 h | 3 h | 3 h |

The pattern “4‑3‑3” gives a dominant 7; “4‑3‑4” gives a major 7, and so on. With this table you can construct any seventh chord by simply counting half‑steps from the root.

---

## 3. Labeling Chord Tones: Root, Third, Fifth, Seventh

Understanding **function** means knowing which note does what inside a chord.

| Label | Role | How It Determines Quality |
|-------|------|----------------------------|
| **Root (R)** | The tonal anchor; defines the chord’s name. | All other tones are measured from here. |
| **Third (3)** | Determines **major** vs **minor** quality. | M3 ⇒ major; m3 ⇒ minor. |
| **Fifth (5)** | Influences **stability**; altered fifths create diminished/augmented colors. | P5 ⇒ stable; d5 ⇒ diminished; A5 ⇒ augmented. |
| **Seventh (7)** | Adds tension and defines **dominant**, **major**, **minor**, or **half‑diminished** character. | m7 ⇒ dominant/minor/half‑diminished; M7 ⇒ major. |

When you see a chord symbol, you can instantly map each note:

- **C⁷** → C (R) – E (M3) – G (P5) – B♭ (m7)  
- **CΔ7** (or **Cmaj7**) → C – E – G – B (M7)  
- **Cm7** → C – E♭ (m3) – G (P5) – B♭ (m7)  
- **Cm7♭5** → C – E♭ – G♭ (d5) – B♭ (m7)

**Inversions** simply reorder these tones, but the labels stay attached to the pitch class, not the position on the staff.

---

## 4. Transposing Triads and Seventh Chords into Any Key

Transposition is the process of moving a chord’s entire intervallic structure to a new root while preserving its quality. Two practical methods are:

### 4.1 Interval‑Counting Method

1. **Identify the chord’s interval formula** (e.g., major triad = 4 h‑3 h).  
2. **Count the same half‑step pattern** from the new root.  

*Example:* Move **E minor (Em)** to the key of **A**.  
- Em formula: 3 h (m3) → 4 h (P5).  
- Starting on A: A → C (3 h) → E (4 h).  
- Result: **A minor (Am)**.

### 4.2 Scale‑Degree Method (Using the Major Scale)

Because you already know how to construct major scales, you can think of chords as built on scale degrees.

| Scale Degree | Triad Quality (in major) | Seventh‑Chord Quality |
|--------------|--------------------------|------------------------|
| I | Major | Major 7 |
| ii | Minor | Minor 7 |
| iii | Minor | Minor 7 |
| IV | Major | Major 7 |
| V | Major | Dominant 7 |
| vi | Minor | Minor 7 |
| vii° | Diminished | Half‑Diminished 7 |

To transpose a **V⁷** chord from C major (G⁷) to D major:

1. Locate the **V** degree in D major → **A**.  
2. Apply the V⁷ quality (dominant 7) → **A⁷** (A – C♯ – E – G).

This method works especially well when you’re already thinking in terms of key signatures.

### 4.3 Quick Transposition Checklist

- **Step 1:** Write the chord’s interval formula.  
- **Step 2:** Write the new root.  
- **Step 3:** Apply the same half‑step pattern.  
- **Step 4:** Double‑check the seventh’s quality (major vs minor).  

If you’re handling **augmented** or **diminished** chords, remember they retain their altered fifths regardless of key—just count the appropriate 4 h or 3 h to the fifth.

---

## 5. Applying the Concepts: A Turnaround in Two Keys

Let’s see the theory in action. You’re accompanying a singer who wants a **blues‑style turnaround** that moves from **C major** to **F major**.

### 5.1 Choose the Basic Progression

A classic **I–vi–ii–V** turnaround in C major:

- **Cmaj7** (I) → **Am7** (vi) → **Dm7** (ii) → **G7** (V)

### 5.2 Build the Chords

| Chord Symbol | Construction (using formulas) |
|--------------|--------------------------------|
| **CΔ7** | C – E (M3) – G (P5) – B (M7) |
| **Am7** | A – C (m3) – E (P5) – G (m7) |
| **Dm7** | D – F (m3) – A (P5) – C (m7) |
| **G7** | G – B (M3) – D (P5) – F (m7) |

### 5.3 Transpose to F Major

Apply the **scale‑degree method**: In F major, the same I–vi–ii–V pattern becomes **FΔ7 – Dm7 – Gm7 – C7**.

- **FΔ7** = F – A – C – E  
- **Dm7** = D – F – A – C  
- **Gm7** = G – B♭ – D – F  
- **C7** = C – E – G – B♭  

Now the progression fits the new key, but the harmonic tension and release feel identical because the interval structures are preserved.

### 5.4 Voice‑Leading Hint (Preview)

Even though voice leading is covered later, a quick tip: keep common tones between successive chords (e.g., the note **C** appears in **CΔ7**, **Am7**, **Dm7**, and **G7**). This makes the turnaround sound smoother and reinforces the learner’s ability to hear the functional relationships you just built.

---

## 6. Practice Exercises

1. **Triad Construction Drill**  
   - Write the notes for a **B♭ augmented** triad and a **E diminished** triad.  
   - Verify each using the half‑step patterns.

2. **Seventh‑Chord Building**  
   - Starting from the root **A**, construct a **dominant 7**, **major 7**, **minor 7**, and **half‑diminished 7**.  
   - Label each tone (R‑3‑5‑7).

3. **Transposition Challenge**  
   - Take the progression **Em7 – A7 – Dmaj7** (ii–V–I in C major).  
   - Transpose it to the key of **G major** using the scale‑degree method.  

4. **Label‑and‑Identify**  
   - Given the chord **F♯m7♭5**, write the interval formula, list the notes, and label each tone (root, third, fifth, seventh).

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Triads** are built by stacking thirds: major (M3‑P5), minor (m3‑P5), diminished (m3‑d5), augmented (M3‑A5).  
- **Seventh chords** add a seventh above the root, with four core types: dominant 7 (M3‑P5‑m7), major 7 (M3‑P5‑M7), minor 7 (m3‑P5‑m7), half‑diminished 7 (m3‑d5‑m7).  
- **Chord tones** (root, third, fifth, seventh) define a chord’s quality and function; the third determines major/minor, the fifth may be altered, and the seventh dictates the seventh‑chord type.  
- **Transposition** preserves interval formulas; you can move any triad or seventh chord to a new root by counting the same half‑step pattern or by using scale‑degree relationships within a major key.  
- Applying these structures in real‑world progressions—such as a I–vi–ii–V turnaround—creates harmonic richness while keeping the underlying logic consistent across keys.

modules.title: Rhythm, Meter, and Tempo
modules.content:
## A Beat‑Driven Story  

Imagine you are sitting in a small jazz club. The pianist launches a solo that feels “laid‑back,” the drummer taps a steady pulse, and the bassist walks a groove that seems to glide between two feels. As a musician, you know the melody, you can name the chords, but something feels off—you can’t quite lock onto **where the beats sit**. This is the moment that rhythm, meter, and tempo step out from the page and become the invisible framework that holds the music together. In the sections that follow, we’ll turn that vague sense of “feel” into concrete skills you can read, count, and internalize.

---

## 1. Mapping Time: Simple, Compound, and Mixed Meters  

### 1.1 What a Time Signature Tells You  

A time signature is a shorthand that tells you two things:

1. **How many beats** are in each measure (the top number).  
2. **What kind of note gets one beat** (the bottom number, e.g., 4 = quarter‑note, 8 = eighth‑note).

When you see **4/4**, you instantly know each measure contains four quarter‑note beats. The same logic applies to **6/8**, **3/2**, etc.  

### 1.2 Simple Meter  

A **simple meter** divides each beat naturally into **two** equal parts. The most common simple meters are:

| Time Signature | Beat Unit | Division |
|----------------|----------|----------|
| 2/4            | quarter   | 2 × eighths |
| 3/4            | quarter   | 3 × eighths |
| 4/4            | quarter   | 4 × eighths |
| 2/2 (cut time) | half     | 2 × quarter‑notes |

**Key point:** In simple meters the beat unit (the note value indicated by the bottom number) can be split cleanly into **two** of the next‑smaller note value.

### 1.3 Compound Meter  

A **compound meter** divides each beat into **three** equal parts. The beat unit is always a dotted note, because a dotted note equals **one and a half** of the next smaller note value (e.g., a dotted quarter = 3 eighths). Common compound meters:

| Time Signature | Beat Unit | Division |
|----------------|----------|----------|
| 6/8            | dotted quarter | 2 × (3 eighths) |
| 9/8            | dotted quarter | 3 × (3 eighths) |
| 12/8           | dotted quarter | 4 × (3 eighths) |

Notice the top number is always a multiple of **3** (but not 3 itself); the bottom number is **8** because the smallest subdivision is the eighth‑note.

### 1.4 Mixed (or Asymmetric) Meter  

**Mixed meters** combine beats of different lengths within the same measure, creating an irregular “feel.” They are most common in progressive rock, folk traditions, and modern classical music. Typical patterns:

- **5/8** – often felt as **2 + 3** or **3 + 2** eighth‑note groups.  
- **7/8** – common groupings: **2 + 2 + 3**, **3 + 2 + 2**, or **2 + 3 + 2**.  
- **9/8** – can be **2 + 2 + 2 + 3** (a “short‑short‑short‑long” feel) or **3 + 3 + 3** (pure compound).

Because the beat unit is still an eighth‑note, you must decide how the beats group together. This decision is usually indicated by the composer or felt through listening.

### 1.5 Quick‑Read Exercise  

> **Score Snippet** (write on staff): 4/4, 6/8, 5/8.  
> **Task**: Count each measure aloud, using “1‑2‑3‑4” for 4/4, “1‑2‑3” for each dotted‑quarter beat in 6/8, and choose a grouping for 5/8 (e.g., “1‑2‑3‑4‑5” with a mental accent on 1 and 3).  

Practicing this simple read‑and‑count routine builds the mental map you need for every rhythmic passage.

---

## 2. Counting Strategies – From “One‑Two‑Three” to Subdivision  

### 2.1 The “Beat‑Talk” Method  

When you first encounter a new piece, **speak the beats** out loud:

- **Simple meters**: Count “1‑2‑3‑4” (or “1‑2” for 2/4).  
- **Compound meters**: Count “1‑2‑3, 4‑5‑6” for 6/8 (each group of three eighth‑notes gets its own number).  
- **Mixed meters**: Break the measure into the smallest logical groups (e.g., for 7/8 felt as 2 + 2 + 3, count “1‑2, 3‑4, 5‑6‑7”).

This vocalization forces your brain to **anchor the primary beats** while still hearing the underlying subdivision.

### 2.2 Counting Subdivisions  

To master syncopation and tuplets, you need a reliable subdivision system:

| Subdivision | Counting Words |
|-------------|----------------|
| **Eighth‑notes** (in 4/4) | “1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &” |
| **Sixteenth‑notes** | “1 e & a 2 e & a 3 e & a 4 e & a” |
| **Triplet eighth‑notes** (in 4/4) | “1‑trip‑let 2‑trip‑let 3‑trip‑let 4‑trip‑let” |
| **Triplet quarter‑notes** (in 6/8) | “1‑trip‑let 2‑trip‑let 3‑trip‑let” |

Having a **consistent verbal grid** makes the invisible pulse audible.

### 2.3 “Clap‑Speak‑Play” Loop  

1. **Clap** the primary beats (e.g., the quarter‑note beats in 4/4).  
2. **Speak** the subdivision (e.g., “1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &”).  
3. **Play** the rhythm on your instrument while maintaining the spoken subdivision.

Repeat until the spoken rhythm and the played rhythm feel inseparable. This loop is especially effective for **syncopated patterns** where notes fall between the primary beats.

---

## 3. Common Rhythmic Patterns  

### 3.1 Basic Motifs  

| Pattern | Notation (in 4/4) | Count |
|---------|-------------------|-------|
| **Quarter‑note + eighth‑note + eighth‑note** | ♩ ♪ ♪ | “1 & 2” |
| **Dotted quarter + eighth** | ♩· ♪ | “1 & 2” (the dotted quarter occupies 1 & 2) |
| **Eighth‑note + rest + eighth‑note + eighth‑note** | ♪ 𝄽 ♪ ♪ | “1 & 2 &” with a rest on “&” after beat 1 |
| **Syncopated off‑beat** | 𝄽 ♪ 𝄽 ♪ | “1 & 2 &” with notes on the “&” of beats 1 and 2 |

These patterns appear in countless styles—from pop to classical. Recognizing them on the page speeds up sight‑reading and improvisation.

### 3.2 Syncopation in Context  

Syncopation occurs when **stress lands on a normally weak part of the beat** (the “off‑beat”). A simple way to identify syncopation:

- Look for notes that **start** on an “&” (the upbeat) **and** **continue** past the next downbeat.  
- Look for **rests** on the downbeat that are followed by a note on the upbeat.

**Exercise:** In a 4/4 measure, write a rhythm that contains **two syncopated notes** and **one rest on a downbeat**. Count it aloud and clap the downbeats to hear the tension.

### 3.3 Rhythmic Ostinati  

An **ostinato** is a repeating rhythmic (or melodic) pattern. In many folk and pop songs, a **four‑beat ostinato**—such as “quarter‑note, quarter‑note, eighth‑note, eighth‑note” (♩ ♩ ♪ ♪)—provides a stable foundation over which melodies and harmonies can shift.

When you encounter an ostinato:

1. **Identify the pattern** and **memorize its count**.  
2. **Lock your foot or tap** to the primary beat while the ostinato repeats.  
3. **Overlay** the melody or harmonic changes on top of the established pulse.

---

## 4. Tuplets: Stretching and Compressing Time  

### 4.1 What Is a Tuplet?  

A **tuplet** groups a number of notes that **do not fit the regular subdivision** of the current beat. The most common is the **triplet**, which packs three notes into the time normally occupied by two.

- **Triplet**: 3 notes in the time of 2 (e.g., three eighth‑notes in the space of one quarter‑note).  
- **Quintuplet**: 5 notes in the time of 4 (e.g., five sixteenth‑notes in the space of one eighth‑note).  
- **Septuplet**: 7 notes in the time of 8, etc.

Tuplets are indicated by a bracket (or “tuplet” number) and often a **small “3”, “5”, “7”** above or below the group.

### 4.2 Counting Tuplets  

Use **distinct syllables** to keep the groupings clear:

| Tuplet | Counting Syllables |
|--------|--------------------|
| **Triplet (eighth)** | “tri‑plet” or “1‑2‑3” |
| **Triplet (quarter)** | “1‑2‑3” (each occupies a third of a half‑note) |
| **Quintuplet (sixteenth)** | “1‑2‑3‑4‑5” |
| **Septuplet (eighth)** | “1‑2‑3‑4‑5‑6‑7” |

Make the syllables **evenly spaced**—the goal is to **fit the entire group into the same time span** as the regular subdivision.

### 4.3 Practical Example: Triplet Feel in 4/4  

Write a **measure of 4/4** that contains:

- Two **eighth‑note triplets** (one on beat 1, one on beat 3).  
- A **quarter‑note** on beat 2.  

**Notation:**  

| Beat 1 | Beat 2 | Beat 3 | Beat 4 |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| ♪♪♪ (triplet) | ♩ | ♪♪♪ (triplet) | — (rest) |

**Counting:** “1‑2‑3 2 4‑5‑6 4 & (hold)”.  

Practice this rhythm with a metronome set to **60 bpm** (one beat per second). The triplet notes should each be **0.667 seconds** apart, while the quarter‑note sits at **1 second**.

### 4.4 Tuplets in Compound Meter  

Because compound meters already divide beats into **three**, adding a **triplet** inside a dotted‑quarter beat creates a **duple‑feel** (two notes in the time of three). This contrast is a frequent expressive device in jazz and Afro‑Cuban music.

**Exercise:** In 6/8, write a measure that contains a **quarter‑note triplet** on the first dotted‑quarter beat, followed by **regular eighth‑note groups** on the second beat. Count it using both the **compound feel** (“1‑2‑3, 4‑5‑6”) and the **triplet feel** (“1‑trip‑let, 2‑trip‑let, 3‑trip‑let”).

---

## 5. Tempo Indications – From Metronome Marks to Expressive Words  

### 5️⃣1. Absolute vs. Relative Tempo  

- **Absolute tempo** is given as a **metronome marking** (e.g., ♩ = 120). This tells you the exact number of beats per minute (BPM).  
- **Relative tempo** uses **Italian words** (e.g., *Allegro*, *Andante*) that convey a general speed range. These terms are often paired with a metronome range in contemporary scores (e.g., *Allegro (♩ = 120–132)*).

Both serve the same purpose: to tell you **how fast the primary beat moves**.

### 5.2 Common Tempo Words and Their Approximate BPM  

| Italian Term | General BPM Range | Typical Mood |
|--------------|-------------------|--------------|
| **Largo**    | 40–60             | Very slow, solemn |
| **Adagio**   | 66–76             | Slow, lyrical |
| **Andante**  | 76–108            | Walking pace |
| **Moderato** | 108–120           | Moderate |
| **Allegro**  | 120–168           | Fast, lively |
| **Presto**   | 168–200+          | Very fast, energetic |

When the composer writes **“Allegro ma non troppo”**, the extra instruction (“but not too much”) refines the tempo—use your ear and the context to find the sweet spot.

### 5.3 Tempo Changes Within a Piece  

- **Ritardando (rit.)** – Gradually **slow down**.  
- **Accelerando (accel.)** – Gradually **speed up**.  
- **A tempo** – Return to the original tempo after a deviation.  

These markings are **relative**; they do not specify exact BPM but tell you how the pulse should move. Practicing them with a metronome set to **tap** the tempo while you slowly adjust the click speed trains your internal sense of acceleration and deceleration.

### 5.4 How Tempo Affects Rhythmic Feel  

Even with the same written rhythm, a **different tempo** can dramatically alter the perceived groove:

- A **slow *Andante* dotted‑quarter rhythm** may feel relaxed, allowing space for expressive rubato.  
- The identical pattern at **Allegro** becomes driving and dance‑like.  

Therefore, **tempo is not just speed**; it shapes the emotional context of the rhythm.

---

## 6. Metronome Mastery – From Steady Pulse to Syncopation  

### 6.1 Setting Up the Metronome  

1. **Choose the beat unit** that matches the time signature’s bottom number (e.g., quarter‑note for 4/4, dotted quarter for 6/8).  
2. **Set the BPM** according to the intended tempo marking. If you only have a word (e.g., *Andante*), start around the middle of its BPM range and adjust by ear.  

### 6.2 The “Pulse‑Only” Drill  

- **Goal:** Internalize the **steady beat** without any melodic or harmonic distraction.  
- **Procedure:**  
  1. Set the metronome to a comfortable tempo (e.g., 80 bpm).  
  2. Clap **only the downbeats** (beat 1 of each measure).  
  3. After 30 seconds, add **off‑beat claps** on the “&”s.  
  4. Finally, try **subdivision claps** (eighth‑notes, then sixteenth‑notes) while keeping the original pulse anchored.  

This drill builds the mental separation between **primary beats** and **subdivisions**, a prerequisite for accurate syncopation.

### 6.3 Syncopation with Metronome  

1. **Select a rhythmic pattern** that contains syncopation (e.g., a quarter‑note rest followed by an eighth‑note on the “&”).  
2. **Program the metronome** to click on the primary beats only.  
3. **Play the pattern** on your instrument, **listening** for the moment when your notes land **between** the clicks.  
4. **Gradually increase** the tempo to test your stability.

### 6.4 Tuplet Practice Using Metronome  

Most metronomes allow you to **set a subdivision** (e.g., click on eighth‑notes while you play triplets). If yours does not, use a **second click track** or a smartphone app that can generate **triplet clicks**.  

- **Step 1:** Set the metronome to the **primary beat** (e.g., quarter‑note at 90 bpm).  
- **Step 2:** While the metronome clicks, **play a series of triplets** on your instrument, aligning the first note of each triplet with the metronome click.  
- **Step 3:** Switch roles—let the metronome click the **triplet subdivision** and play straight eighth‑notes, ensuring each eighth‑note lands on the appropriate triplet click.  

Switching perspectives trains you to **compress and expand** time mentally.

### 6.5 Real‑World Scenario: Preparing a Groove  

You’ve been asked to accompany a singer who wishes to perform a **folk ballad in 5/8** (grouped 2 + 3). Here’s a step‑by‑step plan using the metronome:

1. **Set the click** to a **quarter‑note pulse** at 70 bpm (the “1” of the 2‑beat group).  
2. **Count aloud:** “1‑2 | 3‑4‑5”.  
3. **Clap** the “1” and “3” beats (the start of each grouping).  
4. **Add the eighth‑note subdivision** (1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 &) while keeping the primary claps.  
5. **Play the chord progression** on your instrument, emphasizing the “1” and “3” beats.  
6. **Adjust** the tempo up or down based on the singer’s comfort, always checking that the “2 + 3” feel remains clear.

By the end of the exercise, the irregular meter will feel as natural as a regular 4/4 groove.

---

## 7. Applying Rhythm, Meter, and Tempo in Music  

### 7.1 Sight‑Reading with Rhythm in Mind  

When you encounter a new piece:

1. **Scan the time signature** first.  
2. **Identify any tuplets** (look for bracket numbers).  
3. **Mark the primary beats** with light pencil strokes if needed.  
4. **Count aloud** using the appropriate beat‑talk system before playing a single note.  

This “pre‑parsing” reduces the cognitive load while you actually perform.

### 7.2 Improvisation Over Changing Meters  

If you’re improvising over a **mixed‑meter section**, treat each grouping as a **mini‑phrase**:

- **Phrase 1:** 2 + 2 + 3 → think “short‑short‑long”.  
- **Phrase 2:** 3 + 3 + 2 → think “long‑long‑short”.  

Create melodic kernels that **land on the strong beats** of each grouping, then experiment with syncopated extensions that fall between them. The more comfortable you are with counting each grouping, the more fluid your improvisation will sound.

### 7.3 Compositional Tip: Tempo as a Structural Tool  

When you write a piece, consider **tempo changes** as part of the form:

- **Contrast sections** (e.g., verse vs. chorus) often benefit from a **tempo shift** (e.g., *Andante* → *Allegro*).  
- **Ritardando** at the end of a phrase can give a sense of closure, while **accelerando** into a climax can heighten excitement.  

Use a **metronome** when drafting these sections to ensure the transitions feel natural, not abrupt.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Simple meters** divide each beat into **two**; **compound meters** divide each beat into **three**; **mixed meters** combine uneven groupings.  
- **Counting** with spoken beats (“1‑2‑3‑4,” “1‑2‑3”) and subdivisions (“&,” “e‑a”) anchors your sense of pulse and prepares you for syncopation.  
- **Common rhythmic patterns**—quarter‑eighth‑eighth, dotted‑quarter‑eighth, syncopated off‑beats—appear across styles; learning to read and clap them accelerates sight‑reading.  
- **Tuplets** (triplets, quintuplets, etc.) compress or expand time; use distinct syllables and metronome subdivision drills to internalize them.  
- **Tempo markings** can be absolute (metronome numbers) or relative (Italian terms). Their range influences the emotional character of the rhythm.  
- A **metronome** is essential for mastering steady pulse, syncopation, and tuplets; practice the “pulse‑only,” “syncopation,” and “tuplet” drills regularly.  
- Applying these tools—counting, clapping, metronome work—directly improves sight‑reading, improvisation, and composition across any genre.  

With the beat now firmly in hand, you can move from merely **reading** rhythm to truly **feeling** it, letting time become a partner rather than a constraint.

modules.title: Voice Leading and Cadences
modules.content:
## A Musical Puzzle: Why Does That Chorale Feel “Resolved”?

Imagine you’re arranging a short hymn for SATB choir. The melody lands on the tonic note **C**, but the harmonies you’ve written around it feel flat, as if something is missing. Swap the inner voices, and suddenly the chord breathes—tension releases, and the phrase feels complete. The secret lies in **voice leading** and the way you end phrases with **cadences**. This chapter shows how to move each part smoothly and choose the right cadence to give your music direction and closure.

---

## 1. Voice‑Leading Foundations for Four‑Part Harmony  

Four‑part writing (Soprano, Alto, Tenor, Bass) is the backbone of chorale style and many pop/rock arrangements. The goal is **smooth, logical motion** between chords, preserving each voice’s independence while supporting harmonic function.

### 1.1. The Three Core Principles  

| Principle | What It Means | Typical Application |
|-----------|---------------|----------------------|
| **Stepwise Motion** | Move each voice by a **second** (major or minor) whenever possible. | C‑E‑G → F‑A‑C: soprano moves G → A (step). |
| **Common‑Tone Retention** | Keep a note that belongs to both chords unchanged in its voice. | G‑B‑D (V) → C‑E‑G (I): the G can stay in the soprano. |
| **Avoid Large Leaps** | Leaps larger than a fourth are used sparingly and are usually resolved by step in the opposite direction. | A sudden jump from C to G in the alto should be followed by a step down to F. |

These rules flow naturally from the **intervals** you already studied (Chapter 3) and the **triads** covered in Chapter 4.

### 1.2. Voice‑Leading Between Common Chord Types  

| From → To | Typical Voice Movements | Tips |
|-----------|------------------------|------|
| **I → IV** | 3rd → 2nd (S), 5th → 4th (A), 1st → 2nd (T), 1st → 4th (B) | Keep the **common tone** (the 5th of I) in the alto if possible. |
| **IV → V** | 2nd → 3rd (S), 4th → 5th (A), 2nd → 3rd (T), 4th → 5th (B) | Resolve the leading tone (7th of the scale) in the soprano to the tonic. |
| **V → I** (authentic cadence) | 3rd → 1st (S), 5th → 3rd (A), 2nd → 1st (T), 5th → 3rd (B) | **Root motion** is by fifth (V → I); keep the leading tone in the soprano. |

### 1.3. The “Rule of the Fifth”  

When moving from **V to I**, the **root motion** is a perfect fifth (down) or perfect fourth (up). This interval is the strongest directional force in tonal music. In four‑part writing, the **bass** typically provides this motion, while the upper voices either step or hold a common tone.

---

## 2. Guarding Against Parallel Fifths and Octaves  

### 2.1. Why Parallel Motion Is a Problem  

Parallel perfect intervals (5ths or 8ths) mask the individual lines, making the texture sound **homophonic** rather than **polyphonic**. They also reduce the sense of harmonic tension—essential for a compelling cadence.

### 2.2. Spotting the Pitfalls  

| Situation | Forbidden Parallel Motion | Acceptable Alternatives |
|-----------|---------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Soprano & Alto** both move **G → A** while maintaining a perfect fifth (D‑A) | Parallel 5ths | Split the motion: one voice steps, the other leaps or stays. |
| **Tenor & Bass** both rise a perfect octave (C‑C) | Parallel Octaves | Keep one voice stationary or move by a third. |

### 2.3. Quick Fix Checklist  

1. **Identify common tones** before moving the voices.  
2. **Change one voice** by a step instead of moving both in the same direction.  
3. **Insert a passing tone** in one voice to break the parallel motion.  

*Example*: In a I–V progression, if soprano and alto would both move from G–D to D–A (parallel fifths), let the alto stay on D while the soprano moves to A, creating a **voice exchange** instead of parallel motion.

---

## 3. Authentic (Perfect) Cadences  

An **authentic cadence** is the most decisive sense of closure in tonal music. It occurs when a dominant harmony (V) resolves to the tonic (I). Two sub‑types exist: **perfect** and **imperfect**.

### 3.1. Perfect Authentic Cadence (PAC)  

**Requirements**

1. **Root motion** of the bass: V → I (perfect fifth down or fourth up).  
2. **Soprano ends on the tonic** (the tonic pitch of the key).  
3. **Both chords in root position** (no inversions).  
4. **No voice crossing** (higher voice stays above lower voice).

**Why It Works**  
- The **leading tone** (scale degree 7) in the soprano resolves upward by half step to the tonic, creating a strong pull.  
- The **bass** reinforces the direction with the fifth interval.  

**Major Key Example (C major)**  

| Chord | S | A | T | B |
|-------|---|---|---|---|
| V (G‑B‑D) | B | D | G | G |
| I (C‑E‑G) | C | E | G | C |

*Notice*: Soprano moves B → C (half step), bass moves G → C (perfect fourth up).

### 3.2. Imperfect Authentic Cadence (IAC)  

If **any** of the four conditions above is relaxed (e.g., soprano ends on the dominant, or chords are inverted), the cadence is still authentic but **less final**. Use IACs to create a sense of pause before moving on.

### 3.3. Minor‑Key Authentic Cadences  

In minor keys, the **harmonic minor** scale supplies a raised leading tone (♭7 → ♮7). The V chord is usually **major** (e.g., V = G‑B‑D in C minor). The same voice‑leading rules apply, but be aware of the **modal mixture** (♭6) that may appear in the preceding chord.

**C minor example**  

| Chord | S | A | T | B |
|-------|---|---|---|---|
| V (G‑B‑D) | B♭ | D | G | G |
| i (C‑E♭‑G) | C | E♭ | G | C |

The raised leading tone **B natural** resolves to C, delivering a strong cadence even in a minor key.

---

## 4. Other Cadential Forms  

### 4.1. Plagal Cadence (Amen Cadence)  

**Structure**: IV → I  

- **Common‑tone retention** is the key: the **fourth** of the key (scale degree 4) often stays in the alto or tenor.  
- The **bass** moves a **perfect fourth** down (or fifth up).  

**C major example**  

| Chord | S | A | T | B |
|-------|---|---|---|---|
| IV (F‑A‑C) | A | C | F | F |
| I (C‑E‑G) | C | E | G | C |

Plagal cadences are softer than authentic cadences and work well at the end of a phrase that needs gentle closure (e.g., hymn “Amen”).

### 4.2. Deceptive Cadence  

**Structure**: V → vi (or V → ♭VI in minor)  

- The **soprano** avoids the tonic, typically moving to the **submediant** (scale degree 6).  
- Creates a **surprise** that prolongs tension.  

**C major example**  

| Chord | S | A | T | B |
|-------|---|---|---|---|
| V (G‑B‑D) | B | D | G | G |
| vi (A‑C‑E) | A | C | E | A |

The leading tone B resolves down to A instead of up to C, yielding a deceptive effect.

### 4.3. Half Cadence  

**Structure**: Any chord → V  

- Ends on the **dominant**, leaving the phrase **unfinished** and prompting continuation.  
- Useful for **question‑like** phrasing or to set up a return to the tonic later.  

**C major example**  

| Chord | S | A | T | B |
|-------|---|---|---|---|
| ii (D‑F‑A) | F | A | D | D |
| V (G‑B‑D) | B | D | G | G |

The half cadence’s open-ended feel is reinforced by the **leading tone** in the soprano (F → B) moving toward the upcoming tonic.

---

## 5. Integrating Cadences into Musical Phrasing  

### 5.1. Mapping Cadences to Phrase Structure  

| Phrase Length | Typical Cadence | Effect |
|---------------|----------------|--------|
| **4 bars** | Half Cadence → Authentic Cadence | Creates a question‑answer shape. |
| **8 bars** | Plagal Cadence at bar 8 | Provides gentle finality after a longer development. |
| **12 bars** (blues) | Half Cadence at bar 8, Authentic Cadence at bar 12 | Mirrors the classic twelve‑bar form. |

### 5.2. Using Cadences for Dynamic Shaping  

- **Start with a half cadence** to build anticipation.  
- **Insert a deceptive cadence** in the middle of a development section to keep listeners from predicting the return.  
- **Finish with a perfect authentic cadence** for a decisive closure, or **plagal** for a softer landing.

### 5.3. Voice‑Leading Tips for Cadence Transitions  

1. **Plan the soprano line first** – its movement often determines the cadence type.  
2. **Check the bass** – ensure the root motion follows the fifth/fourth rule for authentic cadences.  
3. **Scan for parallel fifths/octaves** after each chord change.  
4. **Add passing tones** in inner voices to smooth large leaps, especially when moving to or from the dominant.

---

## 6. Practical Exercises  

### 6.1. Exercise 1 – Spot the Parallel Errors  

Write a four‑measure progression in G major: I – vi – IV – V – I.  

- Notate the SATB voices using common‑tone retention.  
- Identify any parallel fifths or octaves.  
- Rewrite the offending voices following the checklist in Section 2.3.

### 6.2. Exercise 2 – Build Cadences  

For the key of **E♭ major**, create three‑measure phrases ending with:  

1. A **perfect authentic cadence**.  
2. A **plagal cadence**.  
3. A **deceptive cadence**.  

Focus on smooth voice leading, especially the soprano’s final note.

### 6.3. Exercise 3 – Phrase Mapping  

Compose an eight‑measure melody in **A minor**. Choose a cadence pattern (e.g., half → deceptive → perfect authentic) and write the accompanying four‑part harmony. Highlight the leading tones and common tones that justify each cadence.

---

## 7. Common Questions  

**Q: Can the soprano skip the leading tone in a perfect authentic cadence?**  
A: No. For a **PAC**, the soprano must end on the tonic, which means the leading tone must resolve upward by half step. Skipping it creates an imperfect authentic cadence.

**Q: Are inversions ever allowed in authentic cadences?**  
A: In a **perfect** authentic cadence, both chords must be in root position. Inverted chords are permissible in an **imperfect** authentic cadence, which sounds less final.

**Q: Do parallel fifths matter in modern pop arrangements?**  
A: The rule originates from classical voice leading, but many contemporary styles intentionally use parallel fifths for a “open” sound. However, if you aim for a traditional chorale or classical texture, avoid them.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Smooth voice leading** relies on stepwise motion, common‑tone retention, and avoiding large leaps.  
- **Parallel perfect intervals** (5ths, 8ths) mask individuality; break them with stepwise motion or passing tones.  
- **Authentic cadences** (perfect vs. imperfect) provide the strongest sense of closure; the soprano must end on the tonic and the bass must move by a fifth/fourth.  
- **Plagal, deceptive, and half cadences** offer softer, surprising, or open-ended alternatives—use them to shape phrasing and maintain interest.  
- Apply the **voice‑leading checklist** before finalizing each chord change: common tones → stepwise motion → no parallel perfect intervals.  
- Practice by constructing progressions, spotting errors, and mapping cadences to phrase structures; the more you internalize these patterns, the more naturally they will appear in your own music.

modules.title: Functional Harmony and the Circle of Fifths
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Hook: The “One‑Four‑Five” Turnaround That Saves a Gig  

You’re backing a singer at a small coffee‑house. After the first verse she cues a familiar “pop‑song feel,” and you instinctively reach for the chord shapes that have carried countless hits: **I–V–vi–IV**. The audience hums along before the lyrics even start. How did you know those four chords would work so well together, no matter whether the song is in C, G, or D? The secret lies in **functional harmony** and the **circle of fifths**—the map that shows how chords pull each other into place.  

In the sections that follow, we’ll unpack exactly why those three functions (tonic, subdominant, dominant) exist, how the circle of fifths orders them, and how you can label any diatonic chord (I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, vii°) in any key. By the end you’ll be able to build classic progressions like **ii–V–I** or **vi–IV–V** on the fly, and you’ll have a toolbox for spotting functional harmony in real songs.

---

## 1. The Three Harmonic Functions  

### 1.1 Tonic – Home Base  

The **tonic** is the harmonic “home” that gives a piece a sense of rest and resolution. In the key of C major, the tonic triad is **C–E–G** (I). Any chord that shares the tonic’s pitch class (C, E, or G) reinforces this feeling, most notably the **vi** chord (A minor) because it contains the same notes as the tonic triad in a different inversion.

*Why it matters*: When a progression lands on the tonic, listeners feel “arrived.” That’s why cadences—especially the perfect authentic cadence (V → I)—resolve to the tonic.

### 1.2 Subdominant – The Departure  

The **subdominant** (IV) introduces motion away from the tonic, creating a gentle tension that begs for further movement. In C major, the subdominant triad is **F–A–C**. The **ii** chord (D minor) also belongs to the subdominant family because it shares two notes with IV (D–F–A) and typically moves toward V or I.

*Why it matters*: Subdominant chords set up the expectation of a dominant resolution. Think of them as the “question” that the dominant will later answer.

### 1.3 Dominant – The Pull Back  

The **dominant** (V) is the strongest force pulling back to the tonic.
